gptr runs a language model agent inside your R session. It computes on objects you already
loaded and keeps named results available for the next iteration. A dataset around 4 GB can
stay in R while the model sees a bounded description and the results its tools report. You
can revise one analysis step without exporting and reloading the dataset for each turn.
The same function, `peter()`, is an interactive chat at the console and a programmable call in
scripts, loops and `if` statements.

The [Execution model](execution-model.html) explains what reaches the provider and what still
costs memory and time. Choose a model in [Language models](language-models.html); the examples
below run offline with a scripted fake provider.

## A first call


``` r
library(gptr)
session = peter("Fit mpg from wt in mtcars. Save the model as fit.", mtcars)
session |> peter("Use fit to predict mpg and plot the predictions.")
```

Peter writes and runs R through its tools. The pipe adds work to the same session, so the next
turn can reuse `fit`.

### Try it offline

This fake provider supplies a fixed sequence of tool calls and replies. It does not infer code
from the prompt.


``` r
library(gptr)

fake = gptr_fake_provider(list(
  list(tool = "r", input = list(
    code = "fit = lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)\ngptr_return(coef(fit))"
  )),
  "Each 1000 lb of weight lowers mpg by about 5.3.",
  list(tool = "r", input = list(
    code = "predicted = predict(fit)\ngptr_return(head(predicted))"
  )),
  "The first six predictions are ready."
))

work = new.env()
session = peter("Fit mpg on wt in mtcars and return the coefficients.", mtcars,
  model = fake, envir = work, mode = auto)
session$text
#> [1] "Each 1000 lb of weight lowers mpg by about 5.3."
session$value
#> (Intercept)          wt
#>   37.285126   -5.344472
```

Prompts are always quoted strings. Identifiers such as the mode can be bare names, the way
`library(gptr)` needs no quotes: `mode = auto` and `mode = "auto"` are the same. The `auto` mode
lets ordinary agent actions run without asking, while retaining the critical and secret guards.
This guide needs it because nobody is there to answer. At the console the default mode,
`manual`, asks before changes unless a permission rule already allows them.

`session$text` is the final answer, and `session$value` is the value the tool selected with
`gptr_return()`.
The object the agent created is in `work`, like any object you created yourself:


``` r
ls(work)
#> [1] "fit"
coef(work$fit)
#> (Intercept)          wt
#>   37.285126   -5.344472
```

Reuse that fitted object in the next turn. No data file or repeated fit is needed:


``` r
session |> peter("Reuse fit to predict mpg and return the first six predictions.")
#> The first six predictions are ready.
#> idle . fake/fake-1 . 2 turns . 6.8k tokens . $0.0000 . sb878545ec1
session$value
#>         Mazda RX4     Mazda RX4 Wag        Datsun 710    Hornet 4 Drive
#>          23.28261          21.91977          24.88595          20.10265
#> Hornet Sportabout           Valiant
#>          18.90014          18.79325
head(work$predicted)
#>         Mazda RX4     Mazda RX4 Wag        Datsun 710    Hornet 4 Drive
#>          23.28261          21.91977          24.88595          20.10265
#> Hornet Sportabout           Valiant
#>          18.90014          18.79325
```

`peter()` returned a session object. It holds the conversation, the model, the status and the
token usage:


``` r
session$status
#> [1] "idle"
session$turns
#> [1] 2
gptr_usage(session, by = "model")
#>   group        requests  input  output  cache_read  cache_write  cost
#> 1 fake/fake-1  4         6769   51      0           0            0
#>
#> # 1 row
#> 4 requests, 6.8k tokens in, $0.0000
```

## The pipe steers one session

Piping a session into `peter()` adds a turn to the same session: the same history, the same
model and the same workspace. This continuation does not duplicate the dataset; ordinary R
code can still allocate copies when it modifies objects or computes new results.


``` r
fake2 = gptr_fake_provider(list(
  list(tool = "r", input = list(
    code = "cyl_mpg = tapply(mtcars$mpg, mtcars$cyl, mean)"
  )),
  "The mean fuel economy per number of cylinders is stored in `cyl_mpg`.",
  "Four-cylinder cars are the most economical, at about 26.7 miles per gallon.",
  "Four."
))

session = peter("Compute the mean mpg for each number of cylinders.",
  model = fake2, envir = work, mode = auto)
session |> peter("Which group is the most economical?")
#> Four-cylinder cars are the most economical, at about 26.7 miles per gallon.
#> idle . fake/fake-1 . 2 turns . 5.1k tokens . $0.0000 . s1d37bb32c9
session$turns
#> [1] 2
session$text
#> [1] "Four-cylinder cars are the most economical, at about 26.7 miles per gallon."
```

A branch is always explicit. `gptr_fork()` copies the conversation into a new session whose
workspace looks up objects in the parent environment and keeps ordinary assignments local:


``` r
branch = gptr_fork(session)
branch |> peter("Answer in one word.")
#> Four.
#> idle . fake/fake-1 . 3 turns . 1.7k tokens . $0.0000 . sca319361b6
c(original = session$turns, branch = branch$turns)
#> original   branch
#>        2        3
```

The overlay separates ordinary bindings, rather than making a full data snapshot. Reference
objects and arbitrary side effects require their usual care; see
[Execution model](execution-model.html).

## Stopping instead of guessing

In `manual` mode a change needs approval unless an allow rule already permits it. When nobody
can answer (an `Rscript` job, a knitted report), the run stops with a classed condition that says
how to allow the action:


``` r
careful = gptr_fake_provider(list(
  list(tool = "r", input = list(code = "mtcars$kpl = mtcars$mpg * 0.425")),
  "Added the column kpl."
))
res = tryCatch(
  peter("Add fuel economy in km per liter to mtcars.", model = careful,
        envir = new.env(), mode = manual),
  gptr_error_permission = function(e) e
)
class(res)[1]
#> [1] "gptr_error_permission"
res$session$status
#> [1] "blocked"
```

`mode = plan` inspects and proposes while preserving the user workspace; level-1 R exploration
can create intermediate objects in its scratch environment. `mode = edits` allows file edits
inside the project, and `gptr_permissions()` adds rules such as `"r(level<=1)"` that allow
low-risk code without a question.

## At the console

Called without a prompt in an interactive console, `peter()` opens a chat. Piping a session
into it continues that session, and `/exit` returns the session. Inside chat, `/help` lists
commands, `@name` attaches an object and `!code` runs your own R immediately.
[Interactive console](interactive-console.html) explains input syntax, permissions and
interrupts.


``` r
peter()
session |> peter()
```

## Connecting a real model

Choose a route explicitly. API providers use their named environment variables, which you can
load from a private file with `gptr_env()`. Subscription CLI routes use the executable's own
sign-in; Ollama uses an already-running local server and an installed model.
[Language models](language-models.html) gives setup examples for each route.


``` r
gptr_env("~/keys/.env")
gptr_providers()
gptr_models(provider = "openai")
gptr_config(model = "openai/gpt-6-sol", .scope = "user")

session = peter("Describe the mpg and wt columns.", mtcars)
session$text
```

The first time a provider is used interactively, gptr shows what is sent to it and records your
acknowledgment; `?gptr_egress` lists what a request contains. For persistent storage, call
`gptr_init("/path/to/project")` to create a `.gptr/` workspace and review its separate trust
decision. Without a project workspace, session storage is temporary. Defaults and storage
policy are covered in [Configuration](configuration.html).
